title: Shore Flies
summary: Shore flies are small dark flies associated with algae and persistently wet greenhouse surfaces. Adults are primarily a monitoring and sanitation signal rather than a direct plant-feeding pest, so they should be distinguished from fungus gnats before management decisions are made.
whatToLookFor: Small dark flies resting or running on wet benches, floors, media surfaces, and areas with algae
Adults with a more robust, moth-like or housefly-like appearance than fungus gnats when viewed with magnification
Larvae associated with algae-rich wet surfaces rather than feeding inside healthy roots
Persistent populations concentrated where drainage, leaks, or chronic surface moisture support algal growth
lookAlikes: Other small flies attracted to moist organic material
Root-zone decline caused by overwatering or pathogens that happens to occur where flies are present
confirmWith: Inspect adults with magnification instead of identifying from flight behavior alone
Compare larval morphology with fungus gnat larvae when immature stages are present
Map captures and sightings against algae, drainage, and wet-surface hotspots
Inspect plant roots separately before attributing crop decline to the flies
managementPrinciples: Correct persistent moisture and algae sources that support reproduction
Use sanitation and drainage correction as the foundation of control
Treat shore-fly presence as evidence to inspect the production environment rather than proof of root feeding
Re-scout wet areas after corrective work to verify that populations are declining
prevention: Prevent chronic standing water and algae buildup
Clean benches, floors, drains, and media spills
Maintain drainage and irrigation systems so surfaces can dry appropriately
Include low, wet greenhouse zones in routine scouting

title: Root-Knot Nematodes
summary: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.) are plant-parasitic roundworms that can reproduce on Cannabis sativa. Hemp studies show that susceptibility and visible galling can vary, so root symptoms should be paired with soil or root testing before the cause is assigned.
whatToLookFor: Root galls, swellings, or distorted fine-root development
Patchy stunting or reduced vigor that may be more severe in heavily infested soil
Reduced root function without a distinctive foliar symptom pattern
Field or media history that includes known root-knot hosts or prior nematode problems
lookAlikes: Crown gall or other abnormal root swellings
Root aphids and other root-zone pests
Compaction, low oxygen, salinity, or irrigation stress
confirmWith: Inspect washed roots for galling and abnormal fine-root structure
Submit representative roots and substrate or soil for nematode extraction and identification
Compare symptomatic and apparently healthy zones instead of sampling one plant
Interpret hemp research cautiously because cultivar and nematode species can change symptom severity
managementPrinciples: Base management on confirmed plant-parasitic nematode presence and species context
Avoid moving infested soil, media, roots, or contaminated equipment into clean zones
Use crop-system-appropriate sanitation, exclusion, and root-zone management rather than relying on foliar symptoms
Track affected zones over time to determine whether pressure is expanding
prevention: Know the nematode history of outdoor sites and reused media systems
Start with clean propagation material and uncontaminated media
Clean soil- or media-contact equipment before moving between zones
Use representative diagnostic sampling when unexplained patchy decline persists

title: Septoria Leaf Spot
summary: Septoria species are documented causes of leaf spot disease on Cannabis sativa. Because foliar lesions overlap with spray injury, nutrient-related necrosis, and other pathogens, lesion appearance should be treated as a starting point for diagnosis rather than a species identification.
whatToLookFor: Discrete tan, brown, or necrotic leaf spots that enlarge or increase in number over time
Lesions that may develop darker margins or small fungal fruiting structures visible with magnification
Disease progression that is more consistent with repeated infection than a one-time injury event
Outdoor or protected-crop conditions that support extended leaf wetness or splash dispersal
lookAlikes: Other fungal or bacterial leaf spots
Mechanical injury and pest feeding scars
confirmWith: Inspect both leaf surfaces and lesion structures with magnification
Record lesion progression and recent wetting or splash events
Compare new lesions with the timing of sprays and environmental events
Use laboratory identification when species-level confirmation affects management or reporting
managementPrinciples: Reduce avoidable leaf wetness and contaminated splash where practical
Remove heavily affected tissue in a way that limits movement of contaminated debris
Improve sanitation and airflow while preserving appropriate crop conditions
Use confirmed diagnosis rather than treating every circular lesion as Septoria
prevention: Inspect incoming and nearby plant material for active leaf spots
Keep irrigation and handling practices from repeatedly wetting foliage where avoidable
Remove diseased debris from production areas
Keep records linking symptom onset to weather, irrigation, and crop movement

title: Neofusicoccum Dieback & Stem Canker
summary: Neofusicoccum parvum has been confirmed as a pathogen of Cannabis sativa and can be associated with stem lesions and terminal dieback. Dieback is not specific to this fungus, so diagnosis should combine stem inspection, crop history, and laboratory confirmation.
whatToLookFor: Progressive terminal or branch dieback that does not match simple water stress
Localized stem lesions, cankers, or discolored tissue associated with declining shoots
Symptoms following wounds, pruning, environmental stress, or movement of infected material
Uneven branch decline while other portions of the plant initially remain functional
lookAlikes: Severe root-zone stress causing secondary shoot dieback
Other fungal canker and dieback pathogens
confirmWith: Inspect the transition between healthy and declining stem tissue
Photograph and sample the advancing lesion margin rather than only dead tissue
Review pruning, sanitation, and plant-movement history
Use a plant diagnostic laboratory for organism identification when confirmation matters
managementPrinciples: Separate suspect material from clean propagation stock
Remove affected tissue or plants where appropriate without spreading contaminated debris
Sanitize cutting tools and work surfaces between plant groups
Correct environmental or mechanical stressors that can compound stem disease
prevention: Use clean propagation stock
Minimize unnecessary stem injury
Maintain tool sanitation during pruning and training
Scout stem lesions and dieback early instead of waiting for whole-plant collapse

title: Sclerotinia White Mold
summary: Sclerotinia-associated white mold has been reported in hemp and cannabis production contexts. White fungal growth and hardened survival structures can be important clues, but laboratory confirmation is appropriate when the diagnosis affects crop-removal or site-management decisions.
whatToLookFor: Water-soaked or collapsing stem and lower-canopy tissue followed by white cottony fungal growth under favorable conditions
Hardened dark survival structures (sclerotia) associated with diseased tissue when present
Localized wilt or stem collapse linked to an infected crown or stem section
Field history involving susceptible crops or persistent soilborne inoculum
lookAlikes: Mechanical stem collapse followed by secondary saprophytic mold
confirmWith: Inspect affected stems and crowns for characteristic fungal growth and survival structures
Document the field or substrate history and distribution pattern
Sample the active disease margin for laboratory identification
Do not identify white mold from white mycelium alone
managementPrinciples: Remove affected material carefully to reduce movement of infected debris
Reduce prolonged moisture conditions that favor disease where compatible with crop needs
Account for persistent soil or debris-borne inoculum when planning future crops
Base site-level decisions on confirmed diagnosis and local agronomic guidance
prevention: Review previous crop disease history before outdoor planting
Remove infected residues rather than incorporating obvious diseased material into clean production areas
Maintain airflow and avoid persistent canopy wetness
Scout lower stems and crowns as well as leaves and flowers

title: Southern Blight
summary: Southern blight, associated with the soilborne fungus commonly called Sclerotium rolfsii (Athelia rolfsii), has been reported on hemp and is favored by warm conditions. Crown collapse and surface fungal growth can resemble other root and stem diseases, so the pathogen should be confirmed when possible.
whatToLookFor: Rapid wilt or collapse associated with a lesion near the soil or media line
White surface mycelium around the crown or nearby substrate under favorable conditions
Small round survival structures that develop from pale to tan or brown as they mature
Disease concentrated in warm areas or sites with a history of susceptible crops
lookAlikes: Heat or drought stress that causes wilt without a crown lesion
confirmWith: Inspect the crown and media surface, not only wilted foliage
Look for fungal growth and survival structures while recognizing they may be absent early
Review temperature, moisture, and field-history context
Use laboratory identification for important outbreaks or uncertain cases
managementPrinciples: Remove severely affected plants and contaminated debris where appropriate
Avoid moving contaminated soil or media into clean areas
Reduce conditions that leave the crown persistently warm and wet when crop requirements allow
Plan future site management around confirmed soilborne disease history
prevention: Know the disease history of outdoor sites and reused growing areas
Use clean media and containers for protected cultivation
Maintain sanitation around plant bases and remove infected residues
Inspect crowns promptly when plants wilt despite adequate root-zone moisture
